paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Why we dream remains one of the great unanswered questions of behavioural science, perhaps the best-known idea is that dreams help us to regulate, analyse, explain and remember major events in our lives, in a kind of mental housekeeping process. Most dreams are based in events from real-life experiences from recent days, suggesting that at least part of their function is to help the brain sort through and make sense of recent experiences. Reliving long-term memories internally through dreams helps to facilitate learning and to reconsolidate memories. Rather than just processing memories in a mechanical way to delete unwanted data from memory, dreams actually appear to refine memories, making them more useful for the future, however, so that the subsequent performance of learned tasks is improved. This has been conclusively demonstrated experimentally — for example, in tests in which rats learn tasks like navigating mazes.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The brain is particularly active during dream-heavy REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep, so it seems logical that REM dreams play an active role in keeping the brain and nervous system in good working order. However, it is becoming increasingly apparent that non-REM dreams may be just as important in facilitating learning as REM dreams. Experiments on rats indicate that during non-REM sleep, activity in the brain largely mirrors that of tasks performed during the previous day, although this is shortened, compressed or speeded up. On the other hand, in the much more detailed dreams of REM sleep (typically five times longer than non-REM dreams), brain-wave activity appears almost identical to that during the original physical experiences, though the tasks are being played out in full.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Because babies and young children spend so much time in REM sleep, it has been proposed that dreams are an essential element in the brain development of infants. The REM sleep of the fetus in the mother’s womb may represent as much as 80% of total sleep time, and a newborn baby spends at least 50% of their sleep time in REM sleep. This percentage continues to fall as the child ages, to around 35% for a one-year-old, before stabilising at around 20-25% in older children and adults. Although the high proportion of REM sleep in young children is well documented, it is less easy to be sure that this REM sleep is actually accompanied by dreams in the very young. Moreover, this particular theory has little to say about the function of dreams in adults.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: As well as their role in memory and learning, some people believe that dreams also help us to resolve emotional problems. Interestingly, recent research has found that sleepers tend to report more negative emotions when waking during REM sleep than during non-REM sleep, suggesting that REM dreams and non-REM dreams may serve different functions in this regard. In particular, the amygdala, which specialises in dealing with unpleasant emotions (e.g. anger, aggression, fear), is very active during REM sleep, and may be involved in the process of resolving emotional issues.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: There is, however, a major school of thought that believes that dreams do not actually serve any natural purpose, and have no significant influence on our waking actions at all. According to this view, dreams are just a random by-product of REM sleep. The peculiar nature of dreams is therefore attributable to certain parts of the brain trying to piece together a story out of what is essentially random information presented to it. This theory might go some way to explaining why dreams are usually so difficult to remember, especially if the brain were to consider them ‘noise’ that we should just forget. This idea that dreams may be instrumental in eliminating certain information is sometimes referred to as ‘active unlearning’. However, the way the brain chooses to interpret these random signals into a story may in itself be considered significant, telling us something about ourselves.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Another interesting view is that new ideas may be created through the generation of random thoughts during dreaming, most of which will likely be discarded as useless, but some of which may be potentially valuable. Some scientists have argued that the brain is fundamentally creative, and that dreams allow this spontaneous creativity to be expressed. However, many purportedly dream-driven discoveries, such as Dmitri Mendeleev's formatting of the Periodic Table and Mary Shelley’s invention of the Frankenstein story are of dubious authenticity. It has been argued that these discoveries were really the product of active waking consciousness reflected in the content of dreams, following few weeks of research, thought and consideration of the issues. It can be argued that the vast majority of discoveries and insights are not dream-related.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Furthermore, many people still believe, like many of the ancients did, that dreams have some prophetic element. However, most alleged successes in predicting the future can be explained by the fact that it is relatively easy to find retrospective connections between dream content and subsequent real events. A more radical idea that has been put forward recently suggests that dreams are not merely a by-product of sleep, but rather what allows us to enjoy the essential healing process of sleep in the first place.

groups.title: The Function of Dreams
content: Scientists still have not fully understood the function of dreams. However, experiments on rats which involve mazes have suggested that dreams may be able to refine our memories.

We also believe that dreams play an important role in how the young child’s {{23}} develops. This idea is supported by the fact that unborn babies spend up to {{24}}% of their sleep time in REM sleep. Unfortunately, studies focusing on this age group are of limited use in studies of {{25}} and their dreams. Nevertheless, recent research has revealed that being woken during REM sleep makes us experience {{26}} that are less positive than if we are woken up during non-REM sleep. This suggests that dreams at these stages have very different functions.
